group.passage: Every word you read on a page or a screen appears in a particular style of letters, known as a typeface. Most readers never give it a second thought, but each style was shaped by a person, a time, and a purpose. Here are the stories behind six well-known typefaces.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Garamond
passage_parts.text: In Paris in the 1500s, Claude Garamond cut metal letters that made books pleasant to read for hours. After his death, his tools were sold and copied across Europe, and versions of his letters still fill the pages of many novels today.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Futura
passage_parts.text: German designer Paul Renner released Futura in 1927. He built its letters from simple shapes such as circles, triangles, and squares, giving them a clean, modern look. In 1969, it was chosen for the plaque that the Apollo 11 astronauts left on the Moon.

passage_parts.label: C
passage_parts.title: Times New Roman
passage_parts.text: In 1932, The Times newspaper in London began printing in a new typeface from Stanley Morison. The paper wanted letters that were easy to read yet narrow enough to fit more words on each line. Times New Roman later became a standard choice for school reports.

passage_parts.label: D
passage_parts.title: Courier
passage_parts.text: IBM asked Howard Kettler to design Courier for its typewriters in 1955. Every letter takes up exactly the same amount of space, so a thin “i” is as wide as a fat “m.” Because IBM did not keep the design to itself, it soon appeared on typewriters everywhere.

passage_parts.label: E
passage_parts.title: Helvetica
passage_parts.text: Created in Switzerland in 1957, Helvetica was meant to look calm and neutral rather than stylish. Its name comes from the Latin word for Swiss, and it is still among the most popular typefaces in the world. It has appeared on New York subway signs, countless company logos, and even the side of America’s space shuttles, though some designers find it boring.

passage_parts.label: F
passage_parts.title: Comic Sans
passage_parts.text: In 1994, Vincent Connare at Microsoft saw cartoon characters in a program speaking in a stiff, formal typeface, so he drew a playful one based on comic books. Comic Sans has been laughed at ever since, yet scientists at a physics laboratory in Europe once used it to announce a major discovery.

questions.stem:
From (A) to (F) above, which typefaces does the passage connect with space travel?
請選出字型前的英文大寫字母，並劃記在答題卷作答區內。（多選題，4分）
Which phrase in (D) means “to fill or occupy a certain area”?（簡答題，2分）

1.strategy_zh: 先看結構：such as 後面列舉兩個例子，空格和 or giving 並列，要填 V-ing。再想「報紙的每一欄塞進更多文字」是哪一則字型的目的，找出那個動詞改成 -ing，注意拼字。

哪一種字型是為報紙設計的？報社希望一行能怎麼樣？
文中的動詞是 fit，改成 -ing 時要重複字尾子音。

2.explanation_zh: (E) 說 Helvetica 至今仍是全世界最受歡迎（most popular）的字型之一；(A) 也說 Garamond 的各種版本到今天還印在許多小說裡，都是「流行了好幾十年」的例子。摘要句 kept their ___ 中，空格在所有格 their 之後，要填名詞，所以把形容詞 popular 轉成名詞 popularity。
evidence: Its name comes from the Latin word for Swiss, and it is still among the most popular typefaces in the world.
After his death, his tools were sold and copied across Europe, and versions of his letters still fill the pages of many novels today.
2.strategy_zh: kept their ___：所有格 their 後面要名詞。再想哪些字型「到今天還很常用」，找出文中描述它「受歡迎」的形容詞，改成名詞。
hints: 哪一則說某個字型到現在仍然名列前茅？用了哪個形容詞？
文中是形容詞 popular，請改成名詞。

3.explanation_zh: (B) 1969 年阿波羅 11 號太空人留在月球上的紀念牌用的是 Futura。(E) Helvetica 曾出現在美國太空梭的機身上。兩者都和太空旅行有關。(F) 是「大意說得通、細節不符」的誘答：歐洲的科學家曾用 Comic Sans 宣布重大發現，容易讓人聯想到太空科學，但文中說的是一間物理實驗室，和太空旅行無關。(A) 書本、(C) 報紙與學校報告、(D) 打字機，都沒有提到太空。

It has appeared on New York subway signs, countless company logos, and even the side of America’s space shuttles, though some designers find it boring.
Comic Sans has been laughed at ever since, yet scientists at a physics laboratory in Europe once used it to announce a major discovery.

option_notes_zh.A: Garamond 一則談的是十六世紀巴黎的金屬活字和今天的小說，沒有提到太空。
option_notes_zh.C: Times New Roman 一則談報紙和學校報告，沒有提到太空。
option_notes_zh.D: Courier 一則談 IBM 打字機和等寬字母，沒有提到太空。
option_notes_zh.F: 科學家用 Comic Sans 宣布重大發現，容易讓人聯想到太空；但文中說的是歐洲的一間物理實驗室（a physics laboratory），不是太空旅行。

hints: 逐則找和太空有關的字，例如 the Moon、astronauts、space shuttles。
有兩則各提到一次太空任務或太空梭。
(F) 的科學家是在哪裡宣布發現的？

A: In Paris in the 1500s, Claude Garamond cut metal letters that made books pleasant to read for hours.
B: In 1969, it was chosen for the plaque that the Apollo 11 astronauts left on the Moon.
C: Times New Roman later became a standard choice for school reports.
D: Because IBM did not keep the design to itself, it soon appeared on typewriters everywhere.

4.explanation_zh: take up 在這裡是「占據（空間）」。(D) 說 Courier 的每個字母都占一樣大的空間（takes up exactly the same amount of space），所以細細的 i 和胖胖的 m 一樣寬。題目的定義「填滿或占據某個範圍」就是這個片語；文中主詞是 Every letter，所以是第三人稱單數 takes up，寫原形 take up 也算對。
evidence: Every letter takes up exactly the same amount of space, so a thin “i” is as wide as a fat “m.”
4.strategy_zh: 定義題：先把定義換成中文「占（多少）空間」，再到 (D) 找說明每個字母寬度的句子；只寫「動詞＋副詞」的片語本身，不要把後面的 the same amount of space 一起抄。
hints: 要找的是「動詞＋副詞」的兩字片語。
在 (D) 找說明每個字母寬度的那一句。
答案的第二個字是 up。

translation_zh.text:
你在紙上或螢幕上讀到的每個字，都是用某一種字母風格呈現的，這叫做字型。大多數讀者從來不會多想，但每一種風格都是由一個人、一個時代和一個目的塑造出來的。以下是六種知名字型背後的故事。

(A) Garamond
十六世紀的巴黎，Claude Garamond 刻出金屬字母，讓書本讀上好幾個小時都很舒服。他死後，他的工具被賣掉，在歐洲各地被仿製；直到今天，他的字母的各種版本仍印滿許多小說的書頁。

(B) Futura
德國設計師 Paul Renner 在 1927 年推出 Futura。他用圓形、三角形和正方形等簡單形狀組成字母，讓它們看起來簡潔又現代。1969 年，阿波羅 11 號太空人留在月球上的紀念牌選用了這個字型。

(C) Times New Roman
1932 年，倫敦的《泰晤士報》開始使用 Stanley Morison 設計的新字型印刷。報社希望字母既好讀，又夠窄，讓每一行能放進更多字。Times New Roman 後來成了學校報告的標準選擇。

(D) Courier
1955 年，IBM 請 Howard Kettler 為公司的打字機設計 Courier。每個字母都占一模一樣大的空間，所以細細的「i」和胖胖的「m」一樣寬。因為 IBM 沒有把這個設計據為己有，它很快就出現在各地的打字機上。

(E) Helvetica
Helvetica 1957 年誕生於瑞士，設計目的是看起來沉穩、中性，而不是追求時髦。它的名字來自拉丁文的「瑞士的」，至今仍是全世界最受歡迎的字型之一。紐約地鐵的標誌、數不清的公司標誌，甚至美國太空梭的機身上都出現過它，不過也有些設計師覺得它很無聊。

(F) Comic Sans
1994 年，微軟的 Vincent Connare 看到一個程式裡的卡通角色用生硬、正式的字型說話，於是參考漫畫書畫出一種活潑的字型。Comic Sans 從此一直被人嘲笑，但歐洲一間物理實驗室的科學家曾經用它宣布一項重大發現。
